evidence_chunks.text: The study reports that PFOS and PFOA affinity to colloidal activated carbon increased as ionic strength rose from 1 to 100 mM and as Ca2+ increased from 0 to 2 mM, indicating promotive effects of higher salinity and divalent cations on adsorption.

Adding 1–20 mg C/L Suwannee River fulvic acid (representing dissolved organic carbon) or 10–100 mg/L diethylene glycol butyl ether (AFFF surfactant) decreased PFOS and PFOA adsorption, showing inhibitory effects of natural organic matter and surfactants.

Co‑contaminants benzene (0.5–4.8 mg/L) and trichloroethylene (0.5–8 mg/L) reduced PFOS adsorption by roughly twenty‑fold at the highest TCE level, while effects on PFOA were neutral to slightly promotive, highlighting PFAS‑specific competitive effects.

The authors conclude that hydrophobic interaction is the predominant mechanism for PFAS adsorption to colloidal activated carbon and that hydrophilic, short‑chain PFAS (e.g., PFBA, PFPeA) will break through barriers first under identical conditions.

evidence_chunks.text: Batch adsorption experiments with Filtrasorb 400 GAC showed that decreasing ionic strength from 10 to 2 mM substantially increased equilibrium PFAS capacities by about 79–146%, indicating inhibitory effects of higher background electrolyte.
At pH 9, equilibrium capacities were modestly reduced (up to 19%) relative to pH 7.7–8.1, suggesting mild pH sensitivity of PFAS adsorption to GAC in the tested range.

Presence of natural organic matter reduced PFAS adsorption capacities, but this negative effect was partially offset when calcium and sulfate were present at constant ionic strength, consistent with competitive sorption and pore-blocking by NOM and charge‑screening by divalent ions.

Multispecies competitive isotherms yielded lower effective solid-phase capacities than single‑solute isotherms, demonstrating strong competitive interactions among co‑occurring PFAS and other solutes in realistic water matrices.

evidence_chunks.text: The authors develop polyethyleneimine‑coated superparamagnetic iron oxide nanocrystals and report ultra‑high sorption capacities for PFOA and PFOS, evaluated in batch systems and bench‑scale sand columns.

They explicitly examine effects of solution pH, ionic composition and strength, and natural organic matter on PFAS sorption performance, showing that water chemistry significantly modulates removal despite strong sorbent affinity.

Quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation measurements provide real‑time interfacial adsorption data, allowing the authors to link changes in PFAS molecular orientation and layer structure to observed matrix‑dependent sorption trends.

Bench‑scale column tests in realistic water matrices demonstrate that, under matched flow and loading conditions, NOM and competing ions reduce breakthrough times relative to clean water, but high capacity and magnetic separation still enable robust treatment.

evidence_chunks.text: Sonochemical treatment of PFOA at 150 W and 40 kHz in water, with or without N2 saturation, achieved less than 25% degradation after 4 hours in the absence of added carbonate radical reagents, showing limited removal in clean water.

Adding NaHCO3 to generate carbonate radicals greatly increased PFOA decomposition and defluorination, with complete degradation achieved within 4 hours under N2‑saturated conditions at an optimal NaHCO3 concentration of about 30 mM.

The authors report that carbonate radical‑assisted sonolysis is most effective at slightly alkaline pH (~8.7), and no shorter‑chain perfluorocarboxylic acids were detected, indicating near‑complete mineralization to fluoride.

evidence_chunks.text: The study examines PFOA photodecomposition under vacuum UV irradiation in the presence of Fe(III), systematically varying reaction atmosphere, added inorganic oxidants, inorganic anions, and organic matter to assess matrix effects.

Inorganic anions hindered PFOA defluorination in the order HCO3− > SO42− > NO3− ≈ Cl− > ClO4−, demonstrating differential scavenging of reactive species and strong inhibition by carbonate and sulfate.
The presence of persulfate in this VUV/Fe system inhibited PFOA defluorination, highlighting complex interactions between oxidant type, radical scavengers, and target PFAS.
